3367.prule: Fixed final (iambic) word stress: in a sesquisyllable the reduced minor syllable is unstressed and the following major syllable is stressed; in a two-element compound the second element is stressed even though the first element is a full, unreduced syllable. Monosyllables are trivially stressed. Position, not syllable weight, decides: the compound examples (kuan ʔiá, lai muóʔ, vu vɨɒ́ʔ, lu lié) have a full first syllable and still take final stress.
3367.srule: Not mentioned in Sun 2020 (sec. 2.1-2.2, p. 287; whole article pp. 285-330): the only stress statements are that the reduced minor syllable is unstressed and the major (final) syllable stressed, with the same iambic pattern in compounds; whether the unreduced first element of a compound keeps any lesser stress is not said.

3367.tone: Source states Lavïa is 'a non-tonal, non-phonational language' (p. 286) with 'total absence of contrastive tone or phonation' (abstract p. 285; concluding remarks p. 306); n. 24 extends the no-tone/no-register claim to the Masan, Zhongke, Yuesong and Yancheng Lavïa varieties (Zhou et al. 2004). Sun notes Drage (1907) 'apparently heard multiple tones' in an unspecified Lavïa dialect (pp. 306-307, citing Diffloth 1980: 23-26) and leaves open whether some Lavïa dialects retain tone or phonation. The sister language Va (Xiyun/Yingla; Sun 2018) is tonal but is a separate Glottolog language (xiyu1235).

3370.dq: stress is understood as an inherent property of a syllable of a word form which consists of the capacity to carry syntactic accentuation. [...] In sum: if a word bears syntactic accentuation, it is generally one particular syllable in the word which stands out. This syllable which can highlight a word by syntactic accentuation carries ‘stress’ (or ‘word accent’, in other terminologies).
3370.dloc: sec. 3 'Regular stress of words of different classes', pp. 11-12
3370.heavy: Source states explicitly that stress is independent of syllable 'weight' (any vowel, with or without onset/coda consonants can carry stress); there is no phonological vowel length in Awetí (p. 26).
3370.prule: Stress falls on the last syllable of the STEM (root), regardless of syllable weight, vowel quality, nasality or word class; the domain is the stem, not the word: nearly all inflectional suffixes (aspect -ju/-(z)oko, mood -(t)u/-aw, negation -(y)ka, all case suffixes) and class-changing derivational suffixes (-(y)tu, -at, -ap) leave stress on the stem-final syllable, so suffixed word forms are typically not word-finally stressed; stress moves to the suffix only with the purposive -°apan, the progressive allomorph -°eju, and class-preserving derivational suffixes (-'at, -ka, -(t)ukat, -tej, -tut, -(p)ut, -(z)ã'jap).
3370.srule: No rhythmic secondary stress: Drude observes no clear pattern of alternating strong and weak syllables and declines to posit trochaic feet (p. 26; p. 32). Secondary stress is reported only on the disyllabic nominal-negation suffix -e'ym, the main stress staying on the stem-final syllable (p. 21, ex. 40: inĩ-e'ym 'no hammock'); speaker-dependently the suffix may take the main stress instead.
3370.quote: As it is the case with many Tupian accent-languages, the stress in Awetí generally falls on the last syllable of the stem. [...] The general rule of stress in Awetí, that the last syllable of the stem carries the stress, is independent of the nasality or other segmental-structural features of the syllables, in particular of their vowel quality and their ‘weight’. This means that syllables with any vowel and with or without consonants in coda or onset position can carry stress. Stress is also independent of the word class. 3372.heavy: Bimoraic syllable = long vowel (two moras on the vowel) or short vowel plus moraic fortis coda; lenis codas carry no mora. This is a stress-to-weight (minimal-word) condition, not a weight-to-stress placement rule.
3372.prule: Tone language (ch. 3: level H and L plus rising and falling contours on nouns, numbered 1/2 in the transcriptions). The only stress content is structural: the phonological word is subject to a minimal-word condition under which the stressed syllable must be bimoraic (fortis codas are moraic, otherwise the vowel lengthens); words are parsed as a single non-iterative trochaic foot with a heavy (branching) head, [μμ] in monosyllables and [[μμ]μ] in disyllables with the head on the first (root) syllable, a rule imported from Sicoli (2007:68) on Western Zapotec and asserted to hold for ZAY on the basis of the author's duration measurements. No stress-placement survey; the author states (p.144) that stress and its phonetic behaviour were not described in detail.

3388.quote: In this section, I provide an overview of the tone system in Bago by defining its distribution, realization and function in nouns and verbs. In the transcription, a high tone is marked by an acute accent, and a low tone is unmarked. Lexically, tone plays an important role in determining the meaning of a word. The following pairs differ in their meanings solely as a result of their tonal patterns. [p. 47] ... In a…
3388.idn: Bago (the Bago language of Bago village; not Kusuntu) (a named variety of the language); data: Bago village, Tchamba district, Central-Eastern Togo, field trips Dec 2015 and May-Aug 2017; Lome 2018 (four months) with principal consultant Shuaib Aboutou; follow-up by phone from Canada
3388.tone: Two-tone register system (H/L), lexically contrastive; contour (falling/rising) tones only on bimoraic syllables (long vowels, nasal codas: 'A falling or a raising contour is never found on a short vowel'); nasals are tone-bearing; mora = TBU; long vowels in verbs always carry one level tone, in nouns a contour may fall on a class suffix (kʊ́d͡ʒɔ-ɔ́, sɔrɔ-ɔ́). Sec. 2.4.1 analyses verbs as H-toned vs toneless with rightward H spread. On stress/accent the source says nothing at all: whole-text a full-text search of the 399-page thesis for stress|stressed|prominen = 0 hits; 'accent' occurs only as 'acute accent' (the tone diacritic); 'prosody' in ch. 3 (pp. 58-59) means syllable-shape correlates of lexical category ([CVN] = verb, [VCV] = noun), not prominence. The thesis neither asserts nor denies word stress.

(104) samara 'ring finger', mehawan 'married', tambu~tambu 'cold', tambambiri 'youth'; vowels under main or secondary stress cannot be deleted.

3389.tone: Cottet classifies Mbahám as a stress language, not a tone or pitch-accent language, but records the competing view (p. 101): 'according to Donohue (2005:48), not only Iha but also Mbahám and Karas, i.e. the whole West Bomberai group, have a pitch accent system'; her answer: 'based on my initial research, I refer to Mbahám as a stress language, keeping in mind that F0 movements are partially unexplained. Tones, if any, have a low functional load in the language.' Conclusion (p. 279): 'Mbahám is a stress language, where stress placement is unpredictable.
